title: A globally convergent primal-dual active-set framework for large-scale convex quadratic optimization
contribution: Adds an auxiliary 'uncertain' index set to the Hintermüller–Ito–Kunisch primal-dual active-set method, which gives finite global convergence on every strictly convex QP while the set stays nearly empty in practice.
problem_entry: The HIK PDAS method is fast but guaranteed only for M-matrix bound-constrained QPs and cycles on others; classical active-set methods are slow at scale; AL/SQO methods need a QP engine (pp. 2-3, 11).
key_idea: The iterates are index partitions. An auxiliary set U of explicitly enforced bounds grows only through change counters (Alg. 5) or a nonmonotone KKT-residual watchdog (Alg. 6), so the method is HIK whenever U is empty (pp. 3, 6-7, 13-16).
assumptions: H positive definite, A full row rank, l < u (by preprocessing); the QP is assumed feasible for the analysis; the HIK result needs a perturbed M-matrix (pp. 4-5, 11).
proof_devices: lemma that a partition whose sets are subsets of the optimal ones yields the exact solution (Theorem 1, p. 8)
finite-state monotonicity: |U| or some counter strictly increases each iteration (Lemma 2 / Theorem 3, pp. 13-14)
nonmonotone watchdog: the max of the last p+1 residuals strictly decreases over finitely many partitions (Lemma 3 / Theorem 4, pp. 15-17)
minimal 3-variable cycling counterexample reused for all strategies (Example 1, Tables 1-3, pp. 11-17)
equivalence to semismooth Newton, with a correction of HIK's superlinear claim (Theorem 5, pp. 27-29; p. 11)
experiments: Matlab + CPLEX + qpOASES. Random BQPs with n up to 1e4 and cond(H) up to 1e6 (50 each), and n = 1e4 QPs with m in {10, 20}. Measures: iterations, linear solves, qpOASES iterations, use of U. HIK failures reported; qpOASES baseline comes with a caveat; q_max and p tuned on the test set (pp. 18-26).
positioning: Calls itself a 'straightforward enhancement' of HIK that is still novel; contrasts in detail with Hager's DASA; corrects a claim in a HIK proof (pp. 3, 9-11).
writing: The contribution is stated in the introduction, followed at once by the practical point that U is usually empty; the worst case is repeatedly 'never witnessed'; hedges are frequent (pp. 3, 14).
limits_future: Weaker with equality constraints (cost of keeping partitions feasible, larger U); recommends classical active-set methods when there are few degrees of freedom; future work: inexact iterative subproblem solves (pp. 25, 27).

method_links.note: Built as the QP engine for AL/SQO; inexact inner solves named as the next step
Minimal hand-built counterexample (n = 3, because n <= 2 provably converges) reused across all strategies
Prints the incumbent's failures and its own weaker equality-constrained results; qpOASES comparison caveated; but q_max and p were tuned on the test set
A single algorithm whose safeguard set grows only on monitored trouble, instead of switching to a classical active-set phase

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The fast unguarded HIK update is the default. The guarantee comes from a monotone finite-state device (U) that is nearly dormant (mu(Last-|U|) mostly 0) and grows by at most one index per iteration
Shows that the fast heuristic is a semismooth Newton method, to inherit its local theory and check claims made about it

transferable: Globalize a fast combinatorial iteration with an auxiliary set that only grows, or with a nonmonotone residual watchdog over a finite state space; convergence then follows from monotonicity or pigeonhole, with no merit function (pp. 13-17)
Prove first that a partition whose sets are subsets of the optimal ones gives the exact solution; each strategy then only needs to reach such a state (Theorem 1, p. 8)
Build the smallest counterexample to the incumbent (one dimension above the provably safe case) and run every variant on it, with iterate tables (Tables 1-3)
Tabulate how much the safeguard is used (average and final |U|, QP-solver iterations against plain linear solves) to show what the guarantee costs (Tables 5-7, 9-11)

quotes.text: We stress, however, that while the proof relies on such worst-case behavior, we have never witnessed such an occurrence in practice.
Variables that change index sets numerous times may be considered sensitive and are prime candidates for membership

title: Iterative reweighted linear least squares for exact penalty subproblems on product sets
contribution: Read in the arXiv v1 preprint ('Matrix-free solvers for exact penalty subproblems'). Proposes IRWA, a matrix-free iterative re-weighting method for convex exact-penalty subproblems over product sets, with global convergence and O(1/eps^2) complexity, and compares it with an ADAL method built for the same setting.
problem_entry: Exact-penalty and convex-composite methods need large subproblems min g'x + x'Hx/2 + dist(Ax+b | C) solved matrix-free; the product structure of C is the entry point (arXiv pp. 1-2).
key_idea: A weighted linear least-squares model with weights (dist^2 + eps_i^2)^(-1/2), solved by CG; the relaxation vector eps is reduced only when the step is small relative to the residual (arXiv pp. 4-5).
assumptions: H positive semidefinite (the indefinite case is excluded); horizon-cone coercivity for cluster points; complexity only for X = R^n, H positive definite and fixed eps; ADAL needs a saddle point (arXiv pp. 2, 7-9, 13, 18).
proof_devices: jointly convex eps-smoothing J(x, eps) and a majorization from the concavity of sqrt(t) that gives descent (Lemma 2.5, arXiv pp. 5-7)
horizon-cone characterization of compact level sets (Theorem 2.8, Corollary 2.9, arXiv pp. 7-9)
subsequence argument: either eps -> 0 or the step test eventually holds (Lemma 2.11, arXiv pp. 9-11)
1/eps Lipschitz bound plus 1/delta telescoping for O(1/eps^2) (Lemma 2.15 to Theorem 2.17, arXiv pp. 13-16)
ADAL rate imported from Wang-Banerjee with a notation-translation table (Remark 3.13, arXiv p. 23)
experiments: Python/SciPy, with CG stopped at a 10% relative residual for both methods. 500 random equality/inequality instances (efficiency curves of CG steps at 50-95% duality-gap reduction), 20 problems of growing size, 40 l1-SVM problems scored by support false positives, and accelerated against plain IRWA. Sensitivity to parameters is admitted (arXiv pp. 27-32).
positioning: In the convex-composite / exact-penalty and IRLS lineage. ADAL is presented as standard technology 'adapted to this setting'. Other ADAL O(1/eps) results are reframed as relying on subproblems as hard as the original (arXiv pp. 1-2, 5, 18, 22).
writing: Calibrated claims ('in certain cases' more reliable; 'perform similarly'); conjectures and open issues flagged as such; theorem-heavy with brief intuition (arXiv pp. 1, 24, 33).
limits_future: No complexity result for the accelerated variants; parameter initialization left to future research; indefinite H excluded; complexity proved only for fixed eps; no test inside an outer loop (arXiv pp. 2, 13, 28, 33).

method_links.note: An inner solver designed for the subproblems of an outer exact-penalty method, matrix-free; but the inner CG uses a fixed 10% relative residual, not a test derived from the outer method, and no outer loop is run
The relaxation vector eps is updated by a progress test (step against residual), with the update rule as the design object, outside the penalty family
The rival ADAL is implemented in the same Python code with the same CG solver and stopping rule; the similar results are printed
Checks other ADAL O(1/eps) claims against what their iterations cost (subproblems as hard as the original)

transferable: Introduce a jointly convex eps-smoothing and show that the reweighted quadratic step is a majorize-minimize descent step on it, using the sqrt(t) concavity bound (arXiv pp. 5-7)
Drive the smoothing parameter down with a step-versus-residual test instead of a schedule, and prove that either eps -> 0 or the test eventually holds (arXiv pp. 5, 10)
Use horizon-cone conditions to get compact level sets, and list easy sufficient conditions (arXiv pp. 7-9)
Compare inner solvers with the same inner linear solver, tolerance and warm start; plot percent solved against total CG steps at several duality-gap reductions (arXiv p. 28)
coauthors: James V. Burke, Hao Wang, Jiashan Wang

quotes.text: The primary novelty of our work is a newly proposed iterative re-weighting algorithm (IRWA) for solving such problems involving arbitrary convex sets of the form (1.3).
More principled methods for initializing and updating these parameters is the subject of future research.

title: Primal-dual active-set methods for isotonic regression and trend filtering
contribution: A block-form PDAS algorithm for isotonic regression with O(n) work, warm-starting and parallelizable merges, plus an adaptive-proportion safeguard (SF2) that makes PDAS reliable on trend filtering.
problem_entry: PAV is O(n) but sequential and cannot be warm-started, which matters for online use and sequences of problems; plain PDAS cycles on trend filtering (pp. 1, 3, 5, 7).
key_idea: The dual of IR is an M-matrix BQP, so HIK PDAS applies. Algorithm 2 runs it in block form with O(1) merges. SF2 moves only a fraction p of the violators and adapts p against the max of a FIFO queue of recent |V| values (pp. 3-4, 7-8).
assumptions: Positive weights; TF with smooth convex f and l1 difference regularizers of order 1-2; SF2 convergence asserted by appeal to [20], not proved (pp. 2, 4-5, 8).
proof_devices: equivalence transfer: the block algorithm generates the HIK PDAS iterates on the dual BQP (Theorem 3.2, p. 4)
work counting with running sums alpha, beta so that each merge is O(1), with at most n merges (p. 4)
cycling counterexample for TF (Example 4.1, Table 1, p. 7)
informal argument for SF2 that the reference value decreases monotonically (p. 8)
experiments: Python 2.7. IR: PDAS against the scikit-learn PAV, 10 instances per n up to 3.3e5, boxplots of time and merges, plus a warm-start perturbation protocol. TF: success rates of PDAS/SF1/SF2 (Table 2), and time and iterations against an IPM written in Matlab, with that handicap stated. Synthetic data only (pp. 8-12).
positioning: Builds on HIK and the authors' own globalized and inexact PDAS; SF1 is taken from Kim-Park and Byrd et al.; PAV's strengths are stated before its drawbacks; the difficulty of warm-starting IPMs is cited (pp. 1, 3, 7, 10).
writing: Workshop-length; argues against the incumbent in the first person; one tiny worked example; promotional conclusion; a typo in update (4) (pp. 3, 5, 7, 12).
limits_future: Parallelism claimed but merges run sequentially; SF2 convergence not proved; synthetic data; cross-language comparison with the IPM; no explicit future work (pp. 8, 10, 12).

method_links.note: A constructed cycling instance for TF is shown before the safeguard is introduced
States the IPM's language handicap and concedes equal merge counts, but timings cross languages, there are 10 instances per size, and safeguard tuning is not reported
Adapts its aggressiveness (the proportion p) from monitored progress instead of switching to a one-index fallback; applied outside the penalty family

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: SF2 changes only a fraction p of the violators and shrinks p only when the queue's reference value fails to decrease
A perturb-and-resolve protocol shows an advantage the incumbents (PAV, IPM) cannot have

transferable: Dualize a structured problem and check whether the dual falls in a class with a known guarantee (an M-matrix BQP); write the algorithm in the primal's structure to inherit the theorem (pp. 3-4)
Keep running sufficient statistics so that each merge costs O(1), and bound the number of merges by n, to prove linear work (p. 4)
Replace a hard switch after t_max failures with action on a fraction p of the violators, adapted against the max of a FIFO queue of recent values (p. 8)
Warm-start protocol: solve a base instance, perturb the data slightly, restart from the old solution, and count the work (pp. 9-10)

quotes.text: However, we argue that the PAV algorithm does have critical drawbacks when it comes to solving large-scale problems of interest today.
This shows that our proposed safeguard, which allows more aggressive updates, can be more effective than a conservative safeguard.

title: A self-correcting variable-metric algorithm for stochastic optimization
contribution: A stochastic BFGS method whose damping weight is the smallest value that enforces the curvature bounds behind BFGS self-correction, with convergence theory, a noise-reduction subroutine derived from that theory, and a limited-memory variant.
problem_entry: Stochastic quasi-Newton methods concentrate on the secant equation and need convexity, two gradients, heavy regularization or Hessian samples; BFGS works because of self-correction, which they ignore (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: v_k = beta_k s_k + (1-beta_k) alpha_k y_k, with beta_k the smallest value in [0,1] satisfying the two Byrd-Nocedal curvature bounds (9); an optional subroutine checks surrogate versions of the analysis conditions (pp. 3-5).
assumptions: Lipschitz gradient, f bounded below. The key conditions (13)-(14) on E[M_k g_k] are admitted to be unverifiable and are complicated by the dependence of M_k on g_k. Strong convexity is added for the rates (pp. 4-5).
proof_devices: recursion for the Byrd-Nocedal potential gamma(H) = tr(H) - ln det(H) (eq. (8), p. 3)
order-statistic averaging: the bounds hold for at least ceil(pK) iterations (Theorem 1, pp. 3-4; proof pp. 10-11)
expected-decrease lemma and Robbins-Monro summability (Lemma 4, Theorem 5, pp. 4-5, 11)
convergence lemma for sequences with summable positive-part increments (Lemma 8, p. 11)
strongly convex case: linear convergence to a neighbourhood, and O(1/k) by induction (Theorem 6, pp. 5, 12)
experiments: Matlab. a1a and rcv1 logistic regression and a 3-layer sigmoid network on MNIST. SC, SC-s, SC-L and SC-L-s against SG and oBFGS/oLBFGS. Budget of max{n, 6400} sample accesses; the same grids for all methods; best-of-grid chosen by lowest final testing loss, from one starting point with single runs. Losses and CPU time tabulated; code public (pp. 6-8).
positioning: Critiques oBFGS, SGD-QN, RES, SQN and SDBFGS by name and mechanism; builds on Powell and Byrd-Nocedal(-Yuan); borrows the SG analysis from Bottou and Bottou-Curtis-Nocedal (pp. 1-5, 11).
writing: Five contribution bullets, opening with a provocative reframing; the theory is called 'motivating'; a practical-considerations subsection admits limits; claims stay within the three problems (pp. 2, 5, 8).
limits_future: Assumptions cannot be verified; the subroutine needs at least two gradients; three test problems, selection on the test set, single runs. Future work: general conditions for adaptive gradient noise reduction (pp. 2, 5-6, 8).

method_links.note: The same tuning grids for all methods, SG included, but best-of-grid on test loss from one starting point and single runs

The damping weight beta_k is set each iteration as the smallest value satisfying a computable test, instead of a fixed regularization; the parameter rule is the contribution, outside the penalty family

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: port the property, not the formula
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Identifies self-correction, not the secant equation, as what makes BFGS work, and designs the stochastic method to preserve exactly the inequalities it needs
beta_k is the smallest value in [0,1] that restores the bounds, so the update is plain (scaled) BFGS whenever possible

transferable: When carrying a deterministic method to the stochastic setting, identify the proved property that makes it work and enforce exactly the inequalities that property needs, with the smallest correction (pp. 2-4)
Damp the curvature pair toward s_k (not H_k s_k) with a weight found by a one-dimensional search on [0,1], so the trace and determinant bounds hold by construction (p. 3)
Turn unverifiable analysis assumptions into runtime tests that use an independent mini-batch gradient as surrogate, within a budget, and skip the update when the budget runs out (p. 5)
Order-statistic step: a bounded average of nonnegative zeta_k implies that at least ceil(pK) of them are below a constant divided by (1-p) (pp. 10-11)
coauthors: none (single author; acknowledges Jorge Nocedal and Daniel P. Robinson)

quotes.text: However, too much emphasis has been placed on this equation.
It is worthwhile to note that the assumption should not be taken lightly since each stochastic gradient influences the value of the corresponding inverse Hessian approximation
